title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and say how many brothers, sisters or children you have.
intro:
Telugu kinship terms are precise: there is no single word for 'brother' or 'sister'. You must say whether they are **older** (*అన్నయ్య*, *అక్క*) or **younger** (*తమ్ముడు*, *చెల్లెలు*) than you, and uncles and aunts differ by which side of the family they are on.

You will also learn the possessive words (my, your, our) and how Telugu sorts nouns into masculine and non-masculine, which decides the form of the verb.

vocab.note: Respectful: అమ్మగారు. Also used to address any woman kindly.
m · short form అన్న; pl. అన్నయ్యలు
Colloquially a wife says మా ఆయన (mā āyana).
Colloquially a husband says మా ఆవిడ (mā āviḍa).
sg. పిల్ల (pilla, child, girl), పిల్లవాడు (boy child)
After names and kin terms: రావు గారు, అమ్మగారు.
Used for family: మా అమ్మ, my mum.

phrases.en: How many people are in your family?
There are five of us in my family.
I have a son and a daughter.

grammar.title: Possessives: my, your, his...
grammar.body:
Possessive words go before the noun, with no extra marker:
నా (nā) my · నీ (nī) your (informal) · మీ (mī) your (polite) · అతని (atani) his · ఆయన (āyana) his (resp.) · ఆమె (āme) her · దాని (dāni) its
మా (mā) our (excl.) · మన (mana) our (incl.) · వాళ్ళ (vāḷḷa) their

For family, Telugu prefers **మా** ('our') even when English says 'my': *మా అమ్మ* (my mum). A name can be used directly as a possessor: *రవి అక్క* (Ravi's elder sister).

To say **mine, yours**, add -ది (-di): నాది, నీది, మీది, మాది. This is also how you say where you are from: *మాది నెల్లూరు* (we are from Nellore).

examples.en: Ravi's elder sister is a doctor.
Our town (yours and mine) is very beautiful.

grammar.title: Gender and plurals: the 'non-masculine' quirk
grammar.body:
Telugu grammar splits nouns into **masculine** (men, boys, male gods) and **non-masculine** (everything else). In the **singular**, women are grammatically grouped with things and animals: *ఆమె వచ్చింది* (she came) has the same ending as *కుక్క వచ్చింది* (the dog came), while *అతను వచ్చాడు* (he came) is different. In the **plural** the split is human vs non-human: *వాళ్ళు వచ్చారు* (they [people] came) but *అవి వచ్చాయి* (they [things] came).

This is purely grammatical; to show respect to a woman you use the respectful pronoun ఆవిడ and the plural verb: *ఆవిడ వచ్చారు*.

Plural is formed with **-లు (-lu)**: పుస్తకం → పుస్తకాలు, అబ్బాయి → అబ్బాయిలు. Nouns in -డు and -ల్లు change: తమ్ముడు → తమ్ముళ్ళు, ఇల్లు → ఇళ్ళు, స్నేహితుడు → స్నేహితులు. మనిషి → మనుషులు (people).

grammar.title: 'I have': dative + ఉండు
grammar.body:
Telugu has no verb 'to have'. Instead you say *to me ... is/are*: the owner takes the **dative** (నాకు nāku, to me; మీకు mīku, to you) and the thing owned takes **ఉంది** (undi, for non-masculine singular) or **ఉన్నారు** (unnāru, people in the plural) or **ఉన్నాడు** (a male). In casual speech the verb is often dropped: *నాకు ఇద్దరు అక్కలు*.

The negative is **లేదు / లేడు / లేరు**: *నాకు అన్నయ్య లేడు* (I don't have an elder brother).

examples.en: I don't have an elder brother.
Do you have a younger sister?

dialogue.title: The family photo
dialogue.setting: Priya shows her colleague Meena a photo on her phone during lunch.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: ఈయన మా నాన్నగారు, ఈమె మా అమ్మ.
lines.roman: īyana mā nānnagāru, īme mā amma.
lines.en: This is my father, and this is my mother.

lines.speaker: Meena
lines.en: Do you have an elder sister?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.native: లేదు, నాకు ఒక చెల్లెలు ఉంది. ఆమె బెంగళూరులో ఉంది.
lines.roman: lēdu, nāku oka chellelu undi. āme beṅgaḷūrulō undi.
lines.en: No, I have a younger sister. She's in Bangalore.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: Yes. My husband's name is Srinivas.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.en: We have a little girl. She's two.

culture: Telugu speakers use kinship terms far beyond the family: an older man is *అన్నా* or *అన్నయ్య* (brother), an older woman *అక్కా* (sister), an elderly man *తాతగారు*, and a shopkeeper might call a young woman *అమ్మా*. Adding *గారు* to a name or kin term (*రావు గారు*, *అమ్మగారు*) is the standard mark of respect. Husbands and wives traditionally avoid each other's names and say *మా ఆయన* ('our he') and *మా ఆవిడ* ('our she').
